evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2016: people with a reported ICD-10 A69 (other spirochetal infections, which includes Lyme disease)
evidence_cards.definition: People with at least one condition record whose 3-character ICD10CDX equals A69.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of unique-person weights (PERWT16F) over the domain; standard error by Taylor linearisation over VARSTR/VARPSU. Person-level, one year only.
comparability: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
MEPS panels overlap across adjacent years: never add or pool these yearly totals.
Condition rows come from household reports coded by professional coders.

AHRQ (MEPS team, 2026-09-24) urges caution forming Lyme cost estimates from MEPS: pooling 2016-2024 gives only about 300-400 observations, expenditures are highly skewed (about 1,000 or more are needed for a solid mean), only treated Lyme is identified (zero-expenditure cases drop out, biasing upward), events may be flagged as arthritis without naming Lyme, comorbidities cannot be separated from Lyme, and onset dates are not recorded. Lyme-specific A69.2 is available only in restricted data centers.

uncertainty.note: Small samples give very wide, unreliable intervals.

evidence_cards.summary: 2016: about 436,208 people (95% CI 250,739 to 621,678; 31 sampled persons) reported a condition coded A69.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check or population context only, never a prevalence of Lyme or Long COVID; not a cost estimate (events are counts, not dollars).

scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This peer-reviewed study analyzes survey data from 4,183 U.S. Lyme disease patients in the MyLymeData registry (3,589 with persistent Lyme disease/PLD, 594 with acute Lyme disease/ALD) to measure how commonly used clinical trial eligibility criteria affect who gets included in research. The document notes a PLD EHR-based study in which adding an antibiotic-prescription eligibility criterion reduced the sample by 85%, but this is cited from an external claims-based study (ref 36), not from this document's own data.

comparison_boundaries: PLD (n=3589, ill ≥6 months post-treatment) and ALD (n=594, ill <6 months) are different case-definition subgroups with different sample sizes and cannot be pooled into a single 'Lyme disease' burden figure.

systemic_gap_caveat.basis: Introduction and Discussion state there is a 'critical lack of clinical guidance for treatment' stemming from the divide between academic researchers and community clinicians, cite a described 'crisis of confidence in the clinical trial system,' and report that only four NIH-funded PLD RCTs have ever been conducted, each excluding 88-99% of applicants (Introduction, p.2; Conclusions, p.11).

decision_relevance.summary: A simulator built from this document could let clinical trial designers, patient advocates, and research funders explore how specific eligibility criteria (CDC surveillance-definition requirement, rash/Western-blot requirement, prior CFS/FMS or psychiatric misdiagnosis exclusion, coinfection exclusion) individually and cumulatively shrink the pool of real-world persistent Lyme disease patients eligible for a trial. Patients and advocates could use it to understand why so few people like them qualify for research, and why treatment guidance remains limited. Care delivery teams could use it to see how the trial-eligible population diverges from the community-treated population. Payers/policy audiences could use it to weigh how restrictive eligibility criteria drive up recruitment time and study cost, though this document supplies no dollar figures to quantify that trade-off directly.
use_cases: Let a user toggle individual eligibility criteria (surveillance-case definition, rash/Western-blot requirement, CFS/FMS or psychiatric misdiagnosis exclusion, coinfection exclusion) on or off and see the resulting projected PLD or ALD sample yield, based on this document's reported prevalence and attrition figures.

Compare the demographic composition (sex, income, region per Table 1) of PLD versus ALD trial-eligible subgroups to flag where a proposed trial's screened population may not represent the underlying patient population.

As a general trial/cohort-design consideration extending beyond what this document itself reports: because the study is about clinical trial eligibility and cohort composition, a simulator could prompt researchers to also screen for unmeasured cohort-level confounders (e.g., home environmental exposures) before attributing treatment-response variance solely to the intervention being studied - this is a general methodological extrapolation, not a finding in this document.

spec.title: Persistent Lyme Disease Trial Eligibility and Patient Burden Explorer (MyLymeData)
spec.boundary: This simulation represents percentage-based findings from a 2022 MyLymeData patient-registry survey: how commonly used clinical trial eligibility rules shrink the pool of eligible persistent Lyme disease (PLD) patients, and how PLD differs from acute Lyme disease (ALD) in prior-misdiagnosis, disability, and self-rated-health prevalence. It omits all dollar costs, caregiving time, and income-loss figures because the source document reports none of these for either group.

takeaway.patient: In this study, only about 1 in 10 people with persistent Lyme disease would qualify for a typical research trial under commonly used rules, often because they were previously misdiagnosed with something else (like chronic fatigue syndrome or fibromyalgia) or diagnosed with a tick-borne coinfection. The study's own modeling suggests that if trials dropped those particular exclusion rules, roughly 6 in 10 people with persistent Lyme disease could potentially qualify instead. People with persistent Lyme disease were also far more likely than those with acute Lyme disease to report being unable to work or rating their health as fair or poor.
takeaway.care: Commonly used eligibility criteria (surveillance-case-definition confirmation, and exclusion for coinfection diagnosis or a prior CFS/fibromyalgia/psychiatric misdiagnosis) leave only about 10% of a real-world persistent Lyme disease population eligible for the kinds of trials this study examined, versus 25% for acute Lyme disease. The study's own modeling finds that loosening the coinfection- and misdiagnosis-related exclusions specifically could raise that to roughly 64%. Persistent Lyme disease patients in this sample also report prior misdiagnosis, coinfection, disability, and poor self-rated health far more often than acute Lyme disease patients.
takeaway.policy: This registry-based study finds that standard PLD trial eligibility criteria retain only about 10% of real-world patients (versus 25% for ALD), and that removing coinfection- and misdiagnosis-related exclusions specifically could raise PLD eligibility to roughly 64% in the study's own modeling. The paper situates this against four historical NIH-funded PLD trials that excluded 88-99% of applicants and took 2.5-4 years to recruit, though it reports no dollar costs for recruitment or care. PLD and ALD subgroups also differ sharply on misdiagnosis, coinfection, disability, and self-rated-health prevalence.

patient: If you have persistent Lyme disease and were previously told you had chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, or a psychiatric condition, this study found that experience is common (74% of its persistent Lyme disease respondents) - you could raise with your clinician whether that history might affect your eligibility for a research study.

Before assuming you don't qualify for any Lyme disease research, ask a patient advocacy organization (e.g., the registry sponsor, LymeDisease.org) whether any current studies use broader eligibility criteria than the ones described here.

If you've stopped working or rate your health as fair or poor, know that this study found these experiences common among persistent Lyme disease patients (28% unable to work; 74% fair/poor health) - you are not an outlier in this sample.
care: This finding - that coinfection diagnosis and prior CFS/fibromyalgia/psychiatric misdiagnosis are the two exclusion criteria doing most of the work in shrinking the eligible pool - may be worth checking against your own practice's intake and referral documentation for Lyme disease patients being considered for research referral.

Consider whether your documentation of tick-borne coinfection diagnoses is structured in a way that would let a trial coordinator later determine eligibility, given how often this criterion drives exclusion in this study.

Given the large PLD-vs-ALD gap in self-reported inability to work and poor health in this sample, this may be a useful prompt to review how disability and functional-status documentation are captured in your own persistent Lyme disease patients' records.
policy: Consider weighing the trade-off the study's own modeling implies: loosening coinfection- and misdiagnosis-related exclusions could raise the eligible persistent Lyme disease pool from about 10% to about 64% in this sample, a factor worth considering when designing or funding future trial protocols.

Factor the historical recruitment timeline this study cites (2.5-4 years for prior NIH-funded persistent Lyme disease trials, each excluding 88-99% of applicants) into planning and budgeting assumptions for new trials, while noting this document supplies no dollar cost figures to quantify that burden directly.

Note that this study's pooled PLD-vs-ALD percentages have not been broken down by sex, age, or race/ethnicity even though the same sample shows a statistically significant sex difference between the two groups; disaggregated analysis using federal survey data could usefully complement this registry's findings.

## Source and scope
Figures come from a peer-reviewed analysis of the MyLymeData patient registry (2022 survey wave), comparing persistent Lyme disease (PLD, illness ≥6 months post-treatment, n=3,589) and acute Lyme disease (ALD, illness <6 months, n=594). The study measures two distinct things that should not be pooled: (1) an 'Attrition Sample' (n=2,396 PLD; n=400 ALD) used to compute cumulative trial-eligibility yield after sequentially applying exclusion criteria, and (2) the full analyzable sample used in Table 2 to compute individual prevalence rates (misdiagnosis, coinfection, disability, self-rated health), each with its own reported denominator. This simulator keeps those two populations in separate inputs/outputs rather than mixing them.

## What is and is not modeled
The document reports no dollar-denominated medical costs, out-of-pocket costs, lost income, or caregiving-time figures for either group, so no cost outputs are included here. All outputs are percentages or percentage-point gaps describing trial eligibility yield and PLD-vs-ALD prevalence differences. The modeled 64% loosened-eligibility figure is the study's own illustrative scenario (removing coinfection- and misdiagnosis-related exclusions specifically), not a guarantee of what any real trial would achieve.

## Limitations
**Subgroup disaggregation:** All percentages here (eligibility yield and Table 2 prevalence rates) are reported only as pooled PLD-vs-ALD values. The same sample shows PLD patients were significantly more likely to be female (81%) than ALD patients (76%, p=0.0053, Table 1), yet the document does not further break down misdiagnosis, coinfection, disability, or health-status findings by sex, age, or race/ethnicity. Federal survey data (MEPS, NHIS, BRFSS) generally supports this kind of disaggregated analysis even though this document did not perform it.

**Systemic gap:** The document describes a structural divide between academic Lyme disease research and community clinical practice: restrictive, often scientifically unjustified trial eligibility criteria exclude roughly 90% of real-world persistent Lyme disease patients, producing small, non-generalizable trials and leaving clinicians, in the authors' words, 'without adequate guidance for treatment.' Only four NIH-funded PLD randomized trials have ever been conducted, each excluding 88-99% of applicants and taking 2.5-4 years to recruit.

MyLymeData is a self-selected, self-reported, non-longitudinal registry; it should not be treated as equivalent to insurance-claims or EHR-based Lyme disease estimates, which the document itself notes would miss the roughly half of Lyme disease patients treated by clinicians whose services are not covered by insurance.

spec.title: Persistent Lyme Disease Trial Eligibility and Patient Burden Explorer (MyLymeData)
spec.boundary: This simulation represents percentage-based findings from a 2022 MyLymeData patient-registry survey: how commonly used clinical trial eligibility rules shrink the pool of eligible persistent Lyme disease (PLD) patients, and how PLD differs from acute Lyme disease (ALD) in prior-misdiagnosis, disability, and self-rated-health prevalence. It omits all dollar costs, caregiving time, and income-loss figures because the source document reports none of these for either group.

takeaway.patient: In this study, only about 1 in 10 people with persistent Lyme disease would qualify for a typical research trial under commonly used rules, often because they were previously misdiagnosed with something else (like chronic fatigue syndrome or fibromyalgia) or diagnosed with a tick-borne coinfection. The study's own modeling suggests that if trials dropped those particular exclusion rules, roughly 6 in 10 people with persistent Lyme disease could potentially qualify instead. People with persistent Lyme disease were also far more likely than those with acute Lyme disease to report being unable to work or rating their health as fair or poor.
takeaway.care: Commonly used eligibility criteria (surveillance-case-definition confirmation, and exclusion for coinfection diagnosis or a prior CFS/fibromyalgia/psychiatric misdiagnosis) leave only about 10% of a real-world persistent Lyme disease population eligible for the kinds of trials this study examined, versus 25% for acute Lyme disease. The study's own modeling finds that loosening the coinfection- and misdiagnosis-related exclusions specifically could raise that to roughly 64%. Persistent Lyme disease patients in this sample also report prior misdiagnosis, coinfection, disability, and poor self-rated health far more often than acute Lyme disease patients.
takeaway.policy: This registry-based study finds that standard PLD trial eligibility criteria retain only about 10% of real-world patients (versus 25% for ALD), and that removing coinfection- and misdiagnosis-related exclusions specifically could raise PLD eligibility to roughly 64% in the study's own modeling. The paper situates this against four historical NIH-funded PLD trials that excluded 88-99% of applicants and took 2.5-4 years to recruit, though it reports no dollar costs for recruitment or care. PLD and ALD subgroups also differ sharply on misdiagnosis, coinfection, disability, and self-rated-health prevalence.

patient: If you have persistent Lyme disease and were previously told you had chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, or a psychiatric condition, this study found that experience is common (74% of its persistent Lyme disease respondents) - you could raise with your clinician whether that history might affect your eligibility for a research study.

Before assuming you don't qualify for any Lyme disease research, ask a patient advocacy organization (e.g., the registry sponsor, LymeDisease.org) whether any current studies use broader eligibility criteria than the ones described here.

If you've stopped working or rate your health as fair or poor, know that this study found these experiences common among persistent Lyme disease patients (28% unable to work; 74% fair/poor health) - you are not an outlier in this sample.
care: This finding - that coinfection diagnosis and prior CFS/fibromyalgia/psychiatric misdiagnosis are the two exclusion criteria doing most of the work in shrinking the eligible pool - may be worth checking against your own practice's intake and referral documentation for Lyme disease patients being considered for research referral.

Consider whether your documentation of tick-borne coinfection diagnoses is structured in a way that would let a trial coordinator later determine eligibility, given how often this criterion drives exclusion in this study.

Given the large PLD-vs-ALD gap in self-reported inability to work and poor health in this sample, this may be a useful prompt to review how disability and functional-status documentation are captured in your own persistent Lyme disease patients' records.
policy: Consider weighing the trade-off the study's own modeling implies: loosening coinfection- and misdiagnosis-related exclusions could raise the eligible persistent Lyme disease pool from about 10% to about 64% in this sample, a factor worth considering when designing or funding future trial protocols.

Factor the historical recruitment timeline this study cites (2.5-4 years for prior NIH-funded persistent Lyme disease trials, each excluding 88-99% of applicants) into planning and budgeting assumptions for new trials, while noting this document supplies no dollar cost figures to quantify that burden directly.

Note that this study's pooled PLD-vs-ALD percentages have not been broken down by sex, age, or race/ethnicity even though the same sample shows a statistically significant sex difference between the two groups; disaggregated analysis using federal survey data could usefully complement this registry's findings.
